blocks.content: A signal is a small, asynchronous notification the kernel or another process sends to a running process, interrupting whatever it happens to be doing at that exact moment. Pressing Ctrl C in a terminal, a program crashing on a bad memory access, and a child process notifying its parent that it has finished are all, underneath, the exact same mechanism: a signal.

This chapter explains what a signal actually is, the small set of signals that come up constantly in practice, the three ways a process can respond to one, and why SIGKILL specifically cannot ever be caught or blocked, a detail that trips people up regularly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297579-970884975.png
1. What a Signal Actually Is

A signal is a small, numbered notification the kernel delivers to a process, either on its own behalf, for something like an invalid memory access, or on behalf of another process explicitly asking to send one, using the kill system call despite its intimidating name. Delivery is asynchronous: a signal can arrive at essentially any point during a process execution, interrupting whatever instruction was about to run next.

Each signal carries no real payload beyond its own identity, just a number and a name, SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, and so on. What matters is not data being transmitted, it is the simple fact that a specific, predefined kind of event has happened and the target process needs to know about it right away.

3. Three Ways a Process Can Respond
blocks.text: 3. Three Ways a Process Can Respond

blocks.content: When a signal arrives, a process handles it in exactly one of three ways. It can accept the default action the kernel defines for that particular signal, which for many signals means terminating immediately. It can run a custom handler function it registered ahead of time, giving it a chance to react in its own specific way. Or it can explicitly choose to ignore the signal entirely, in which case nothing observable happens at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297580-73444767.png
blocks.alt: Three Ways a Process Can Respond

blocks.content: 4. Why SIGKILL Cannot Be Caught, Blocked, or Ignored
blocks.text: 4. Why SIGKILL Cannot Be Caught, Blocked, or Ignored

blocks.content: SIGTERM is deliberately a polite request. A process can register a handler for it, use that handler to flush buffers, close files cleanly, save state, and only then actually exit on its own terms. This cooperative behavior is exactly why SIGTERM, not SIGKILL, is the standard default signal sent by tools like the kill command with no explicit flags.

SIGKILL is different by deliberate design. It cannot be caught by any handler, cannot be blocked, and cannot be ignored, under any circumstances. The kernel terminates the target process immediately and unconditionally, with zero opportunity for that process to run any cleanup code at all. This exists specifically as a last resort, a guaranteed way to stop a process that is unresponsive, stuck, or refusing to honor a gentler SIGTERM request.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297581-507255452.png
blocks.alt: Why SIGKILL Cannot Be Caught, Blocked, or Ignored

blocks.title: Why this distinction matters in practice
blocks.content: Sending SIGKILL first, out of impatience, skips any chance for the target process to save state or clean up properly. The standard, correct practice is to send SIGTERM first and give the process a real opportunity to exit gracefully, only escalating to SIGKILL if it genuinely fails to respond.
5. Asynchronous Delivery: Interrupting Normal Execution

A defining property of signals is that they can arrive at essentially any point in a process execution, not at some predictable, scheduled moment. A process can be in the middle of an ordinary loop, a system call, or any other normal code, and a signal handler, if one is registered, runs immediately, temporarily taking over execution before the interrupted code eventually resumes.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297581-249647698.png
6. SIGCHLD: The Signal Behind Proper Zombie Reaping
blocks.text: 6. SIGCHLD: The Signal Behind Proper Zombie Reaping

blocks.content: SIGCHLD deserves special attention here because it directly connects this chapter back to the zombie processes chapter. Every time a child process terminates, the kernel automatically sends SIGCHLD to that child parent, specifically to notify it that a child has finished and its exit status is now available to be collected.

A well written parent registers a SIGCHLD handler that calls waitpid in a loop every time it receives this signal, reliably collecting every finished child promptly and automatically. This is precisely the correct fix for zombie accumulation described in that earlier chapter, rather than a parent having to poll for finished children manually.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297581-765257536.png
blocks.alt: SIGCHLD: The Signal Behind Proper Zombie Reaping

blocks.content: 7. Signal Masking: Temporarily Blocking Delivery

Sometimes a process is in the middle of a critical section, forward pointer to the synchronization module concept of the same name, and genuinely cannot afford to be interrupted by a signal handler right at that moment. Signals support exactly this need through masking: a process can temporarily block a specific signal from being delivered.

Blocking a signal does not discard it if it arrives during the blocked period. It is instead marked pending, held by the kernel, and delivered immediately the moment the process unblocks that signal again. This gives a process a reliable way to protect sensitive code from interruption without ever silently losing a signal that arrived during that protected window.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297582-269788709.png
8. Sending Signals from the Command Line
blocks.text: 8. Sending Signals from the Command Line

blocks.content: The kill command, despite its name, is a general purpose tool for sending any signal to a process by its PID, not just for forceful termination. Signals can be specified either by number or by name.

9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming SIGKILL and SIGTERM are basically interchangeable ways to stop a process, when only SIGTERM allows the target to clean up first, and SIGKILL cannot be caught or blocked under any circumstances.","Believing a blocked signal is simply dropped or lost, when it is actually held as pending and delivered as soon as the process unblocks it.","Forgetting that kill sends a signal generically, and by default that signal is SIGTERM, not necessarily a forceful kill in the everyday sense of the word."]
items: Assuming SIGKILL and SIGTERM are basically interchangeable ways to stop a process, when only SIGTERM allows the target to clean up first, and SIGKILL cannot be caught or blocked under any circumstances.
Believing a blocked signal is simply dropped or lost, when it is actually held as pending and delivered as soon as the process unblocks it.
Forgetting that kill sends a signal generically, and by default that signal is SIGTERM, not necessarily a forceful kill in the everyday sense of the word.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely why SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, and to connect SIGCHLD directly back to how zombie processes get reaped correctly. Both are extremely common follow up questions once fork and exec have already been covered.

Signals are the asynchronous notification layer running underneath process management on any Unix like system, tying directly into the fork, exec, zombie, and orphan chapters that came before this one. The next chapters move on to pipes and shared memory, the mechanisms processes use to actually exchange data with each other, not just notifications.
